stories.institution: Beijing Tiantan Hospital / China National Clinical Research Center for Neurological Diseases, AI stroke clinical decision support system (GOLDEN BRIDGE II)
stories.teaser: AI helps doctors prevent a second stroke
stories.headline: AI decision support cut new strokes and other vascular events across 77 Chinese hospitals
stories.why: Cluster randomised trial of 21,603 patients at 77 hospitals in China, The BMJ
stories.bullet: 26% lower risk of new vascular events, with AI stroke care in 77 hospitals
texts:
At 77 hospitals across China, 21,603 people with ischaemic stroke were treated either with usual care or with help from an AI decision support system that reads MRI scans, classifies the stroke's cause and recommends prevention treatment.

After three months, new vascular events were 2.9% against 3.9%, a 26% lower adjusted risk. The cluster randomised trial is in The BMJ.

#AIforGood

After a stroke, the next danger is another one. In a trial led by Beijing Tiantan Hospital, an AI system helped doctors at 38 Chinese hospitals choose prevention treatment by reading brain scans and working out what caused each stroke.

Their patients had fewer new strokes, heart attacks and vascular deaths, and the gap held at 12 months: 4.0% against 5.5%.

#AIforGood

Can software help doctors prevent a second stroke? A trial at 77 Chinese hospitals tested it with 21,603 patients.

Hospitals given an AI system for scan reading, stroke classification and treatment advice scored higher on care quality, 91.4% against 89.8%, and saw fewer new vascular events at three months and at a year.

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: Effect of a clinical decision support system on stroke care quality and outcomes in patients with acute ischaemic stroke (GOLDEN BRIDGE II): cluster randomised clinical trial

stories.institution: University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (SAVE-O2 AI trial), autonomous oxygen titration with the O2matic PRO100 at four U.S. hospitals
stories.teaser: AI keeps hospital patients' oxygen in the safe range
stories.headline: AI-controlled oxygen kept hospital patients in their target range 85% of the time, against 63% with standard care
stories.why: Randomized trial of 300 adults at four U.S. hospitals, JAMA Internal Medicine
stories.bullet: 85% of time in the safe oxygen range, as AI adjusted patients' oxygen flow
texts:
Oxygen is one of the most common hospital treatments, yet it is still mostly adjusted by hand. In a randomized trial of 300 adults at four U.S. hospitals, led by CU Anschutz, an AI system adjusted the flow on its own.

Patients spent 85% of the time in their target oxygen range, against 63% with standard care. The results are in JAMA Internal Medicine.

#AIforGood

Too little oxygen harms patients, and so does too much. Nurses and doctors do their best to keep levels right, but readings can change in minutes.

In the SAVE-O2 trial, an automated system adjusted oxygen in real time for hospitalized adults. Both low and high oxygen levels became less common, staff made fewer manual adjustments, and serious adverse events did not rise.

#AIforGood

What if a patient's oxygen adjusted itself, second by second? A CU Anschutz-led trial at four U.S. hospitals tested exactly that with 300 adults.

With the AI system, patients stayed in their target oxygen range 85% of the time, against 63% with clinicians adjusting by hand. The device maker had no role in the study.

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: CU Anschutz-Led Trial Finds AI System Improves Oxygen Delivery in Hospital Patients

stories.institution: Changhai Hospital, Naval Medical University (Shanghai) with partner hospitals, KITE-CRM AI risk support for cystic renal masses on CT
stories.teaser: AI spares patients surgery on harmless kidney lesions
stories.headline: AI help with kidney CT scans cut treatment of harmless lesions by more than half in a randomized trial
stories.why: Randomized implementation trial of 5,869 adults in China, eClinicalMedicine
stories.bullet: Benign lesions treated fell from 40% to 16%, with AI reading kidney CT scans
texts:
When a CT scan shows a cyst-like mass in the kidney, doctors must judge whether it might be cancer. In a randomized trial of 5,869 adults led by Changhai Hospital in Shanghai, scans were reported with or without an AI risk tool.

Among lesions that went on to treatment, 16.4% turned out benign with AI, against 40.3% without it. The study is in eClinicalMedicine.

#AIforGood

An operation on a kidney lesion that turns out to be harmless carries all the risk and none of the benefit. In a trial led by Changhai Hospital in Shanghai, an AI tool helped doctors judge cystic kidney masses on CT.

Fewer than 1 in 100 patients in the AI group were treated for a benign lesion, against about 3.5 in 100 with standard reporting.

#AIforGood

Can AI spare patients an operation they never needed? A randomized trial in China tested it with 5,869 adults whose CT scans were reported with or without an AI risk tool for cystic kidney masses.

Treatment of harmless lesions fell by more than half: 16.4% of treated lesions were benign with AI, against 40.3% without.

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: CT-based AI risk support for cystic renal masses: multicenter validation, reader study, and a randomized implementation study

stories.institution: Vanderbilt University Medical Center, AURA (AUtoimmune Risk Assessment) model in the electronic health record
stories.teaser: AI speeds autoimmune diagnoses for high-risk patients
stories.headline: An AI risk model cut the median wait for an autoimmune diagnosis from 138 days to 43 at Vanderbilt
stories.why: Pragmatic randomized trial of 2,385 patients with a positive ANA test, NEJM AI
stories.bullet: Diagnosis in 43 days instead of 138, as AI flagged high-risk ANA results
texts:
A positive ANA blood test can signal lupus or another autoimmune disease, but most people who test positive do not have one. At Vanderbilt University Medical Center, an AI model in the health record scored each patient's risk, and high-risk patients were invited for a fast-track rheumatology visit.

In a randomized trial of 2,385 patients, median time to diagnosis fell from 138 days to 43.

#AIforGood

Waiting months for answers about an autoimmune disease means months without the right treatment. Vanderbilt tested a different path: an AI model that spots which patients with a positive ANA test are most at risk, so they can be seen sooner.

In a two-year randomized trial published in NEJM AI, patients were diagnosed in a median of 43 days, against 138 with usual care.

#AIforGood

What if the patients most likely to have lupus were seen first? Vanderbilt built an AI risk model into its electronic health record and tested it in a randomized trial of 2,385 people with a positive ANA test.

Those invited for expedited rheumatology care were diagnosed in a median of 43 days, against 138 days in the usual-care group.

#AIforGood
stories.og_title: Randomized Evaluation of an Autoimmune Disease Prediction Model - AURA (AUtoimmune Risk Assessment)

options.headline: THE RIGHT CARE, AT THE RIGHT TIME
options.text: Every story below is a randomized trial, and each one is about a decision. Which prevention treatment to give after a stroke. How much oxygen a patient needs, minute by minute. Whether a kidney lesion needs an operation. Which patients with a positive blood test should see a specialist first. In each case AI helped, and patients got better-matched care: fewer new strokes, steadier oxygen, fewer needless operations and faster diagnoses.

options.headline: WHAT IF EVERY CALL HAD A SECOND OPINION?
options.text: Medicine runs on judgment calls. What happens when AI offers a second view? Four randomized trials below give real answers: fewer new strokes and other vascular events across 77 Chinese hospitals, oxygen kept in the safe range far more often, treatment of harmless kidney lesions cut by more than half, and autoimmune diagnoses in 43 days instead of 138. Where would a second opinion help you most?

options.headline: HELP THAT SERVES THE HEALER
options.text: Purpose in medicine is the patient in front of you. The trials below show AI serving that purpose rather than replacing it. Doctors still choose the stroke treatment, decide on surgery and see the patient with the worrying blood test. AI sharpens the picture and takes on the constant small adjustments, like keeping oxygen steady, so clinicians can put their attention where it matters most.

options.headline: THE EVIDENCE IS IN
options.text: Worries about AI in medicine are loud, and some are fair. The answer is evidence, and the stories below bring it: four randomized trials, more than 30,000 patients in total, each comparing AI-supported care with usual care. The results: fewer new vascular events after stroke, oxygen kept on target, fewer needless kidney operations and faster autoimmune diagnoses.

options.headline: FOUR TRIALS, FOUR GAINS
options.text: Four randomized trials, four measured gains: fewer new strokes and other vascular events in China, steadier oxygen in U.S. hospitals, fewer needless kidney operations in a Shanghai-led trial, and autoimmune diagnoses three times faster at Vanderbilt.
